title: Product Engineering Lab
tagline: Three interface primitives — a command palette, a spatial canvas, explorable charts — built to be imported by a stranger, not demoed.
role: Solo — library design, build pipeline, showcase

hero.alt: The Product Engineering Lab landing page, introducing the library of primitives
hero.caption: The showcase is a demo site, not a component dump.

problem: Most component playgrounds are a drawer of unrelated widgets: each one demonstrates that something can be rendered, none of them is something you would actually install. I wanted the opposite — a small set of primitives that share a design system, a build pipeline and a standard, where the package is the deliverable and the showcase is just how you look at it.
data: Four rules, set before any code and applied to every package. Headless first, so the logic lives in pure functions and hooks and the presentation is swappable. A stated performance budget, proved rather than asserted. Accessibility as a requirement, not a later pass. And a written case study for each primitive explaining the one interesting trade-off it makes.
built: Three primitives and the design tokens that connect them. A command palette with typed async providers, shown driving a fake issue tracker so you can see a real product respond rather than a widget in isolation. A spatial canvas engine handling pan, zoom-toward-cursor, marquee selection and culling, with a live counter showing how many of a thousand nodes are genuinely mounted. And a set of explorable data-viz primitives — an activity heatmap, a zoomable timeline, and a brushable scatter of 290 Swedish municipalities.
Every package has the same three layers: a pure core with no React, hooks that own state and input, components that render.

images.alt: A command palette open over a mock issue tracker, showing ranked results grouped by pages, actions, issues and people
images.caption: The palette searches pages, actions, issues and people in one ranked list — the headless hook is the product, the component is one way to dress it.

images.alt: A knowledge graph laid out in clustered space on the canvas engine, with a heads-up display reporting mounted versus culled nodes
images.caption: A thousand nodes in clustered space. The HUD reports what is actually in the DOM, because only on-screen nodes exist.

images.alt: A scrolling data story combining an activity heatmap, a milestone timeline and a brushable scatter plot
images.caption: Three chart primitives over one pure data layer, each framed as a story rather than a demo.

result: Three primitives finished and two more designed but not built — listed as planned rather than quietly implied. 211 tests across the workspace, none of them snapshots, and every component suite runs an accessibility check over its own rendered output.
technical: The test suite has two layers. Pure cores — fuzzy ranking, zoom-to-cursor maths, scales, hit-test geometry — are tested as plain functions. Components are driven through real input, with assertions going through accessible roles and names, so a test fails when the user-visible contract breaks rather than when markup is refactored.

jsdom has no layout engine, no `ResizeObserver` and no `PointerEvent`, which normally means charts silently render at zero width and the tests pass anyway. A shared test package installs shims that report a real box and let a test change it, so responsive behaviour and culling are genuinely exercised.

Packages build through tsup to ESM plus type declarations, with a `"use client"` banner so they drop straight into a Next.js server tree. Storybook aliases the packages to their source rather than their build output — a choice I A/B tested rather than assumed, and documented in the README along with what it costs.
